hints: Start by measuring the length of line A-B on your printed Fig. 6.1 in mm with a ruler. This is your image size, I.
Convert that mm measurement to nm so units match the actual size, then use $M = I / A$ with $A = 1400$ nm to find magnification.
walkthrough:
Measure the Image Size**
You are sitting with the micrograph, so first get the image size. Place a ruler along line A-B. On most printouts this is about 13 to 15 mm, typically about 14 mm. That is I in the formula.

Match Units Then Divide**
Magnification only works if I and A are in the same units. Actual size A = 1400 nm. Convert image to nm: $1$ mm = $1,000,000$ nm, so $14$ mm = $14,000,000$ nm. Then $M = I / A = 14,000,000 / 1400 = \times 10,000$. Always show working and write magnification with a $\times$ sign.
Final answer: Measure A-B = approx. 14 mm = $14,000,000$ nm. $M = 14,000,000 / 1400 = \times 10,000$ (accept approx. $\times 9286$ to $\times 10714$ for 13-15 mm).

hints: Look closely at chromosome C in Fig. 6.1. How many thick rods are joined together, and is the narrow waist exactly in the middle or slightly off-centre?
Recall what a metaphase chromosome is made of after DNA replication. What are the two identical halves called and what holds them together?
Think about the special DNA at the very tips that protects the ends during replication. Where would you place that label?
Remember chromosomes are not just shape. What molecules make them up, and how would you show a gene as a small region on one arm?
walkthrough:
Get the Shape Right**
Chromosome C is a metaphase chromosome, so DNA has already replicated. Draw two parallel sister chromatids side by side, joined at a constriction. In Fig. 6.1 the constriction is not central, so make one pair of arms shorter than the other. That shows a non-metacentric chromosome.

Add the Core Labels**
Label one whole rod as sister chromatid. Label the narrow joining region as centromere. Label the very tip of a chromatid as telomere. Telomeres must be at the end, they are protective repetitive DNA that stops loss of coding DNA.

Show Composition and a Gene**
For extra credit, annotate that chromatids consist of DNA wound around histones, and draw a small band across one chromatid labelled gene / allele. A gene is not a dot, it is a length or section of DNA at a locus.

Final answer: Drawing of chromosome C showing two sister chromatids joined at a slightly off-centre centromere (non-metacentric). Label: sister chromatid, centromere, telomere at end of chromatid, and DNA + histones / gene as a section of chromatid.

hints: Think about what happens to chromatin between prophase and metaphase for thickness, and where all the chromosomes sit in the cell at metaphase for focusing.
walkthrough:
Why Metaphase Gives the Clearest View**
During prophase to metaphase, chromatin supercoils and condenses to its maximum thickness, so individual chromosomes become distinct instead of a tangled mass. At metaphase they are also all lined up on the equator plate, meaning they are in one plane and in focus together for counting and imaging.
Final answer: Chromosomes are most condensed / thickest and all lie on the equator in one focal plane, so clearly visible.

hints: Recall the order prophase, metaphase, then what? Think of the stage when sister chromatids separate to opposite poles.
walkthrough:
Next Stage After Metaphase**
The mitotic sequence is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Once chromosomes are aligned at the equator, centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles by spindle fibres. That separation stage is anaphase.
